content: Progestogen-only pills (POPs), also known as progestin-only pills or mini pills, are contraceptive medications that contain synthetic progestogens (progestins) but do not include estrogen. Despite being referred to as Progesterone Only Pills, they do not contain natural progesterone but rather chemically related compounds. There are various formulations of progestogen-only contraceptives available. The mechanism of action of progestogen-only contraceptives depends on the dose and activity of the progestogen. Traditional very low-dose progestogen-only pills, as well as subdermal implants like Norplant and Jadelle and intrauterine systems like Progestasert and Mirena, inhibit ovulation inconsistently in approximately 50% of menstrual cycles. Their primary contraceptive effect is achieved by thickening cervical mucus, which reduces sperm viability and penetration. Intermediate-dose progestogen-only contraceptives, such as the progestogen-only pill Cerazette or the subdermal implant Implanon, allow some follicular development but inhibit ovulation more consistently, in 97–99% of cycles. These also cause similar changes in cervical mucus. High-dose progestogen-only contraceptives, such as injectable forms like Depo-Provera and Noristerat, completely suppress follicular development and ovulation, while also inducing the same cervical mucus changes as lower-dose formulations. In cycles where ovulation does not occur due to progestogen-only contraceptives, the endometrium becomes thin and atrophic. If the endometrium is similarly thin and atrophic during an ovulatory cycle, it could theoretically interfere with the implantation of a fertilized embryo (blastocyst). The theoretical efficacy of progestogen-only pills is comparable to that of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs). However, POPs are taken continuously without breaks between packets, and traditional formulations must be taken at the same time every day with a stricter time window (within 3 hours) compared to COCPs (12 hours). In some countries, the POP Cerazette has an approved 12-hour window. The real-life effectiveness of POPs depends heavily on user compliance. Unlike COCPs, POPs are not reliant on gut bacterial flora for absorption and are therefore unaffected by antibiotic use. However, their efficacy can be compromised by episodes of diarrhea or vomiting. Progestogen-only pills offer several benefits. Since they do not contain estrogen, they are not associated with an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or cardiovascular disease. The absence of estrogen also makes them a safer option for individuals with sickle-cell disease. Additionally, the low dose of progestogen and lack of estrogen make POPs safe for use during breastfeeding, and they may even enhance milk production. Like combined pills, POPs reduce the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease. However, it remains unclear whether POPs provide the same level of protection against endometrial and ovarian cancers as COCPs. Side effects of progestogen-only pills include irregular bleeding patterns, particularly in the initial months of use. Most women eventually experience light spotting at relatively regular intervals. Other potential side effects include breast tenderness (mastalgia) and mood swings. Weight gain is less commonly reported with POPs compared to COCPs. The relationship between progestogen-only pills and breast cancer risk is less well-studied than that of COCPs due to smaller populations of POP users. A large 1996 reanalysis of studies on hormonal contraceptives and breast cancer risk found that current or recent POP users had a slightly increased relative risk (RR 1.17) of breast cancer diagnosis, which was not statistically significant. This relative risk was similar to that observed in COCP users (RR 1.16). As with COCPs, the increased relative risk associated with POPs diminished over time after discontinuation, disappeared after 10 years, and was consistent with earlier detection or the promotion of preexisting cancer growth. A 1999 evaluation by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) reviewed the 1996 reanalysis and four case-control studies of POP users included in the analysis. The IARC concluded that there was no evidence of an increased risk of breast cancer with progestogen-only contraceptives, but due to inadequate evidence, they classified them as possibly carcinogenic. Concerns about the role of progestogens in the increased breast cancer risk associated with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in postmenopausal women, as observed in the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trials, have not extended to the use of progestogen-only contraceptives in premenopausal women.
